chapter_theme: Petty understanding (புல்லறிவாண்மை): the small-minded scorn the teaching of virtue, see life slipping away and still do no good, nurse quarrels, hoard and put things off, until old age or death leaves them nothing. Folly is measured here by wasted time and wasted wealth.
structure_note: 321 and 322 are a pair of images for failing to taste good teaching: the ladle and the tanner's dog. 323 to 325 deal with conduct among others. 326 to 330 deal with wealth and years spent without virtue, ending with Death taking the people one loves.

321.reading: The learned take as real worth the words of loving people who teach virtue out of compassion; the fool, himself of no worth, mocks them, as a ladle cannot taste the milk-rice it stirs.
321.nuance: The ladle is in the milk-rice all the time and tastes nothing: being near good teaching is not the same as taking it in. Mudaliar takes பொருளல்லா ஏழை as a fool of no account, and Shanmuganar as one who does not grasp the real meaning.

322.reading: When those free of crookedness explain the way of virtue, those not rightly disposed do not hear it even when they lend an ear, just as the tanner's dog that chews leather cannot take the taste of milk-rice.
322.nuance: Mudaliar reads அவ்வியம் as crookedness of mind, or as envy standing for every bad trait. The image draws on a caste occupation: Mudaliar glosses குணுங்கர் as புலையர்.

323.reading: What does it matter whether they die or live, those dull and shameless people who see in every way that their dear life may leave in the blink of an eye, and still do not a millet grain's worth of good?
323.nuance: Mudaliar lets நன்றி mean any good deed, or specifically help given to others.

324.reading: The days left are few, life has no safeguard, and the blame that many spread is everywhere; why then should anyone, among so many, refuse to smile with those he meets and stand apart nursing a private enmity?
324.nuance: The case against sullen enmity rests on shortage of time rather than on virtue: with life brief and unsafe, hostility is a waste. Mudaliar lets ஏமம் mean pleasure as well as protection.

325.reading: If a man goes before a gathered assembly and reviles another, and the one reviled stays silent, it is a wonder if the reviler survives.
325.nuance: The verse doesn't say how the reviler is undone. Pope supplies a reason, that abuse is the reviler's life and silence stops his mouth. The commentators say only that he will not prosper.

326.reading: One who does not eagerly take up virtuous deeds and work at them before old age comes on will be pushed aside in his own house and told 'sit outside, go away' even by the maidservant.
326.nuance: The penalty is social, not karmic: humiliation in old age, inside one's own home.

327.reading: People of petty understanding neither enjoy their wealth nor do good to the deserving nor join the good path that protects; dazed and sunk in their prosperity, they spend their days for nothing.
327.nuance: Mudaliar names the cause of the daze: not knowing that body and wealth do not last.

328.reading: Fools who do not tie on tightly, early in life, the provisions for the road they must take, but tighten their grip on their wealth and say 'we will see to it later', will find that the gold they point to with their hands turns into a sour vilam fruit.
328.nuance: The commentators fill in a deathbed scene: the dying man, unable to speak, gestures for gold to give away, and his family takes the gesture to mean a sour vilam fruit. Mudaliar quotes a Civaka Cintamani verse telling this story. The quatrain gives only the gesture and the sour fruit.

329.reading: In poverty and in grave illness the small-minded think of the next world, but once they are able to act they give it not a mustard seed's worth of thought.
329.nuance: The irony is that concern for the next life arrives only when one is least able to act on it.

330.reading: Alas, though they have gained this human body they do not think of virtue and waste their days, even while they watch Death preparing to take those they love beyond measure, as dear as their own lives.
330.nuance: Shanmuganar calls the human body hard to obtain; the verse's இவ்வுடம்பு implies as much without saying it.

links.note: Both use milk-rice whose taste goes unknown: the ladle that stirs it and the dog that prefers leather.
415 makes the words of the good a staff on slippery ground; in 321 the learned value such words while the fool mocks them.
Both describe hearing that isn't hearing: 418's ear unpierced by instruction is deaf though it hears, and 322's listeners lend an ear and still do not hear (செவிகொடுத்தும் கேட்கலார்).
Both end on the same verdict, 'what matter whether they die or live'. The Kural aims it at those who taste with the mouth and not the ear; 323 at those who see death coming and do no good.
999 says the world is dark even by day for those who cannot laugh with others; 324 asks why anyone would refuse to smile with those he meets.
158 tells one to defeat those who wrong one out of arrogance by one's own forbearance; 325 shows that defeat in public, though it doesn't name forbearance.
326 shows the cost of putting off virtue until old age; 332 names the usual excuse, that the household's needs come first.
1006 names the same two failures, not using one's wealth and not giving to the deserving. 327 adds a third: not taking the good path that protects.
Both picture the end, when the tongue no longer works. 335 urges good deeds before that moment; 328 shows the gesture that comes too late.
Both mock the words of postponement: பின்னறிவாம் here, மற்றறிவாம் in 332.
333 says wealth doesn't stay, so do lasting deeds as soon as you have it. 329 shows people who think of such deeds only when their means are gone.
336 states the general fact that one here yesterday is gone today. 330 makes it the death of one's own loved ones and still finds people unmoved.

new_concepts.gloss: the next world or life, for which good deeds are provision
new_concepts.label_source: The text's word: quatrain 329 names மறுமை twice, and Mudaliar uses it in glossing 328.
